description: In the KeyG2SigG1 configuration of github.com/cloudflare/circl/sign/bls, bls.Verify and bls.VerifyAggregate decode the attacker-supplied signature into a G1 point without rejecting the identity. That point is fed, alongside the honest H(m), into ProdPairFrac, whose batch-affinization helper (affinize) has no z=0 handling: one identity input zeroes the running z-product, Fp.Inv(0) silently returns 0, and every G1 input — including H(m) — is mapped to the off-curve point (0,0,1). The Miller loop on such points produces values confined to Fp2, and the final exponentiation sends any nonzero Fp2 element to 1, so the pairing-product check passes. The attacker therefore needs only the constant 0xC0 || 0x00×47 to forge single or aggregate signatures over arbitrary messages and honest keys.
reproduction: 1. Construct sig = 0xC0 followed by 47 zero bytes (compressed G1 point-at-infinity).
2. Submit sig alongside any chosen message to a verifier using bls.Verify[bls.KeyG2SigG1] with the victim's genuine public key.
3. Verifier decodes sig to the G1 identity, affinize zeroes all G1 inputs, pairing product evaluates to GT identity, Verify returns true.
4. For aggregates, submit the same 48-byte constant as aggSig with any list of (pk_i, m_i); VerifyAggregate returns true.
technical_details:
Hi --

I've found a universal-forgery bug in CIRCL's BLS signature verifier.

A fixed 48-byte string (0xC0 followed by 47 zero bytes) is accepted by

bls.Verify and bls.VerifyAggregate as a valid signature on any

message, under any honestly-generated public key. This affects one of

the two configurations the package exports (short signatures); the

other is not affected by this mechanism. The attached Go program

generates two fresh keypairs and shows the constant accepted under

both, and as an aggregate.

(Up-front disclosure: an LLM found this bug. I validated the bug myself,

and have confirmed the PoC works to the best of my understanding.

I stand by this report myself personally and vouch for its correctness.)

Separately, this is one of five CIRCL findings from the same scan I

ran. The others are less severe. I could either send them over all to

you right away without manual validation, or if you'd prefer we can

have them validated first but this will take a bit more time. If you

can let me know what you'd prefer I'll go with whatever is better for

you.

No onto the bug. But first a caveat: while I do have a degree in math,

and understand the below to a certain extent, I can't be confident in

the explanation that follows. I am very sure the bug is real and is as

bad as I think it is---because the verification program is about as

easy as possible to interpret---but the technical details are somewhat

beyond me. I'm providing them in the hope they will help you

understand what is going on.

BLS signatures on the BLS12-381 curve come in two symmetric

configurations, depending on which of the curve's two point groups (G1

or G2) holds the signature and which holds the public key. CIRCL

exports both: KeyG1SigG2 puts signatures in G2 (96 bytes) and keys in

G1 (48 bytes), and KeyG2SigG1 does the reverse, with 48-byte signatures

and 96-byte keys. The latter is the "minimal-signature-size" variant, and

the 48-byte string above (0xC0 0x00 0x00 ... 0x00) is the standard

compressed encoding of G1's point at infinity.

A bilinear pairing e(P, Q) takes one point from G1 and one from G2 and

returns an element of a third group, GT. To sign, the holder of a

secret scalar x computes sigma = x * H(m), where H hashes the message

to a curve point.  The public key is pk = x * g, with g the fixed

generator of the other group. Verification checks

    e(H(m), pk)  ==  e(sigma, g)

which holds for an honest signature because both sides equal

e(H(m), g)^x by bilinearity. Rather than compute two pairings and

compare them, it's standard to compute one divided by the other and

check that the result is the identity element of GT. That way the

expensive "final exponentiation" step at the end of a pairing only has

to run once on the product instead of once per pairing.

CIRCL's Verify (sign/bls/bls.go) does exactly that. It builds a

two-element list of G1 points and a parallel two-element list of G2

points, and hands them to ecc/bls12381.ProdPairFrac, a helper that

takes lists P[], Q[], and a list of +/-1 signs, and returns

    prod_i  e(P[i], Q[i]) ^ sign[i]

with a single final-exponentiation over the whole product.

For KeyG2SigG1 the signature and the hashed message are both G1 points,

and the public key and generator are both G2 points. So Verify sets up

(bls.go:301-306):

    G1 list:  [ H(m), sigma ]      --- sigma is the attacker's bytes

    G2 list:  [ pk,   g2    ]

    signs:    [ +1,   -1    ]

and returns true iff ProdPairFrac of those is the GT identity, i.e.

e(H(m), pk) * e(sigma, g2)^-1 == 1.

The signature bytes are decoded into the sigma slot by G1.SetBytes

(ecc/bls12381/g1.go), which explicitly recognises the

compressed-infinity encoding:

    isInfinity := int((b[0] >> 6) & 0x1)

    if isInfinity == 1 {

        ...

        g.SetIdentity()

        return nil

    }

After decoding the signature, Verify calls pub.Validate(), the

method on the caller-supplied PublicKey that checks the public key is

not the identity and is in the right subgroup (bls.go:158-168). That

guards the *key*. Nothing analogous is done for the deserialised

*signature* point. So the G1 list passed to ProdPairFrac is [H(m), O],

where H(m) is honest and O is the identity (x=0, y=1, z=0 in projective

coordinates).

This fact on its own is not a forgery. Mathematically, e(O, g2) = 1, so

the pairing product should be e(H(m), pk) * 1, which is not the

identity for an honest key. The bug is in how ProdPairFrac prepares its

inputs.

Curve points are carried around in projective coordinates (x, y, z),

which represent the affine point (x/z, y/z); the Miller loop inside the

pairing wants them in affine form (z = 1). Converting one point means

computing 1/z, and field inversion is expensive (hundreds of

multiplications) so the first thing ProdPairFrac does

(ecc/bls12381/pair.go:119) is convert the whole G1 list at once:

    affineP := affinize(P)

affinize (g1.go:401-425) uses a standard batch-inversion trick

(Montgomery's trick): multiply all the z-coordinates together, invert

the product once, then peel it apart with a few multiplications per

point so that each point gets divided by its own z. N points costs

1 inversion + ~3N multiplications instead of N inversions. But the

routine has no special case for z == 0:

    ws[0].SetOne()

    for i := 0; i < len(points); i++ {

        ws[i+1].Mul(&ws[i], &points[i].z)       // running product of z's

    }

    w := &ff.Fp{}

    w.Inv(&ws[len(points)])                     // invert the product

    ...

    for i := len(points) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {

        zinv.Mul(w, &ws[i])

        w.Mul(w, &points[i].z)

        out[i].x.Mul(&points[i].x, zinv)        // x * zinv

        out[i].y.Mul(&points[i].y, zinv)        // y * zinv

        out[i].z.SetOne()                       // z = 1

    }

If any input has z = 0, then the running product is zero. Because

Fp.Inv (ff/fp.go:131) is implemented as a fixed sequence of squarings

and multiplications that computes x^(p-2), on input zero every

intermediate value is zero, and Inv(0) silently returns 0 rather than

erroring. w is therefore 0, zinv is 0 for every iteration, and *every*

output point (including the honest H(m)) comes out as (0, 0, 1).

That point is not the identity (it's not even on the curve), but the

Miller loop (pair.go) does not check this either. Computing a pairing

has two stages: a "Miller loop" that walks the bits of a fixed scalar

and, at each step, squares an accumulator in GT and multiplies in a

"line value" that depends on the two input points; and then a "final

exponentiation" that raises the Miller result to a fixed huge exponent

to land it in the right subgroup of GT. GT here lives inside Fp12 ---

the degree-12 extension of Fp, which you can think of as twelve Fp

coordinates arranged as six coefficients from Fp2 on powers of a formal

variable w (1, w, w^2, w^3, w^4, w^5). Fp2 is the "constant term"

subfield --- the Fp12 elements where all the w-coefficients are zero.

CIRCL's line-evaluation (pair.go:48-67) stores the result as

a[0] + a[1]*w^2 + a[2]*w^3, where each a[i] is an Fp2 value, and

a[1], a[2] are computed by multiplying something by P.x and P.y

respectively. With P.x = P.y = 0, those two terms are zero, and only

a[0] in Fp2 survives. The Miller accumulator starts at 1 (an Fp2

element), and multiplying or squaring Fp2 elements stays in Fp2 --- no

w-terms appear out of nowhere. So after both Miller loops, the

accumulated product sits entirely in Fp2.

The final exponentiation then maps any nonzero Fp2 element to 1. A

pairing's final exponentiation raises to (p^12 - 1)/r, and

implementations conventionally split that exponent into an "easy" half,

(p^6 - 1)(p^2 + 1), which is cheap because raising to p is the

Frobenius map (a coefficient shuffle), and a "hard" half that costs

real work. CIRCL's finalExp (pair.go:69-73) calls

EasyExponentiation (ff/cyclo6.go:67-82) then HardExponentiation. The

easy part raises to (p^6 - 1)(p^2 + 1). The nonzero elements of Fp2

form a group of size p^2 - 1, and p^2 - 1 divides p^6 - 1; so any

nonzero Fp2 element raised to p^6 - 1 is already 1, and the rest of the

exponentiation keeps it at 1. res.IsIdentity() at bls.go:321 returns

true. Verify returns true.

bls.VerifyAggregate (sign/bls/bls.go:363-432) is the API for checking

one "aggregate" signature over n (public-key, message) pairs --- the

property that makes BLS attractive: n signatures can be added together

and verified with one call. It builds the same kind of parallel lists,

length n+1 this time, and calls the same ProdPairFrac. For KeyG2SigG1,

listG1 holds [H(m_1), ..., H(m_n), aggSig] (bls.go:411-424), where

aggSig is again decoded with SetBytes and not identity-checked. One

z = 0 entry in that list zeros the whole batch-inversion, so the same

constant 0xC0 00...00 passes as a valid aggregate over any set of keys

and messages.

The KeyG1SigG2 variant is not affected by this mechanism. There the G1

list is [pk, g1], but the public key has already been validated to be

a non-identity at bls.go, so the batch product is never zero. The

attacker-controlled signature is a G2 point and reaches miller

directly, where an identity G2 input is handled correctly.

The narrowest fix is in sign/bls/bls.go, right after decoding the

signature: reject if the decoded G1 or G2 point is the identity,

mirroring what pub.Validate() already does for keys. I've attached a

patch that does this in both Verify and VerifyAggregate.

The deeper fix is in ecc/bls12381/g1.go affinize: either skip z = 0

entries in the running product and emit the canonical identity for

them, or fall back to per-point toAffine() when the batch product is

zero. Without this, any other caller of ProdPairFrac or ProdPair that

mixes an attacker-supplied G1 point with honest ones has the same

problem. I've attached a second patch for affinize as well.

I've tested both against circl at 9798df7 on go1.22, and verified

they prevent the PoC from succeeding. But honestly this is just Claude

telling me what to do, I don't really understand what I should be doing.

Thanks, and please let me know if you'd like to discuss anything,

Nicholas

Below are steps to reproduce this on a stock Linux box with Go >= 1.21:

  git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/circl.git

  cd circl

  mkdir -p /tmp/blspoc && cd /tmp/blspoc

  cat > main.go <<'EOF'

  package main

  import (

      "crypto/rand"

      "fmt"

      "github.com/cloudflare/circl/sign/bls"

  )

  func main() {

      infSig := make([]byte, 48)

      infSig[0] = 0xC0

      ikm1 := make([]byte, 32); rand.Read(ikm1)

      ikm2 := make([]byte, 32); rand.Read(ikm2)

      sk1, _ := bls.KeyGen[bls.KeyG2SigG1](ikm1, nil, nil)

      sk2, _ := bls.KeyGen[bls.KeyG2SigG1](ikm2, nil, nil)

      pk1, pk2 := sk1.PublicKey(), sk2.PublicKey()

      m1, m2 := []byte("msg one"), []byte("msg two")

      real := bls.Sign(sk1, m1)

      fmt.Println("[NORMAL ] Verify(pk1, m1, real)  =",

bls.Verify(pk1, m1, real))

      fmt.Println("[NORMAL ] Verify(pk1, m2, real)  =",

bls.Verify(pk1, m2, real))

      fmt.Println("[EXPLOIT] Verify(pk1, m1, O_G1)  =",

bls.Verify(pk1, m1, infSig))

      fmt.Println("[EXPLOIT] Verify(pk1, m2, O_G1)  =",

bls.Verify(pk1, m2, infSig))

      fmt.Println("[EXPLOIT] Verify(pk2, m1, O_G1)  =",

bls.Verify(pk2, m1, infSig))

      fmt.Println("[EXPLOIT] VerifyAggregate(..)    =",

          bls.VerifyAggregate([]*bls.PublicKey[bls.KeyG2SigG1]{pk1, pk2},

                              [][]byte{m1, m2}, infSig))

      // control: KeyG1SigG2 is NOT affected

      skA, _ := bls.KeyGen[bls.KeyG1SigG2](ikm1, nil, nil)

      pkA := skA.PublicKey()

      infG2 := make([]byte, 96); infG2[0] = 0xC0

      fmt.Println("[CONTROL] KeyG1SigG2 w/ O_G2     =",

bls.Verify(pkA, m1, infG2))

  }

  EOF

  go mod init blspoc

  go mod edit -replace github.com/cloudflare/circl=$HOME/circl

  go mod tidy && go run .

  # [NORMAL ] Verify(pk1, m1, real)  = true

  # [NORMAL ] Verify(pk1, m2, real)  = false

  # [EXPLOIT] Verify(pk1, m1, O_G1)  = true

  # [EXPLOIT] Verify(pk1, m2, O_G1)  = true

  # [EXPLOIT] Verify(pk2, m1, O_G1)  = true

  # [EXPLOIT] VerifyAggregate(..)    = true

  # [CONTROL] KeyG1SigG2 w/ O_G2     = false
title: CIRCL sign/bls: universal signature forgery in KeyG2SigG1 via G1-infinity point
